[/workspace/elastic.md] lines 1-75 of 75
 1|# Elasticsearch telemetry
 2|
 3|Query this cluster by passing `connector_id: "nightshift-evals-telemetry"` to `nightshift_sandbox_bash`.
 4|Credentials are not stored here: for that single command only, the environment contains
 5|
 6|- `CONNECTOR_CONFIG_URL` — Elasticsearch URL
 7|- `CONNECTOR_HEADER_AUTHORIZATION` — full Authorization header value (`ApiKey <key>`)
 8|
 9|Reference those variables directly and never hard-code their values. A command that omits
10|`connector_id` gets no credentials and cannot reach Elasticsearch.
11|
12|Readable indices: `logs-orcabench.otel-*`, `traces-orcabench.otel-*`, `metrics-orcabench.otel-*`.
13|
14|## Query guidance
15|
16|- Use the readable patterns above in place of `logs-*` in the example below.
17|- Name each remote explicitly as `remote:index`; never use wildcard remote names in
18|  `_resolve/cluster`, `_cat/indices` or searches. Use `GET /_remote/info` only if remote names
19|  are not supplied above. To check many remotes, query them in parallel with a short
20|  per-request timeout, as in the last example below: a sequential loop over dozens of remotes
21|  exceeds the sandbox command timeout and returns nothing.
22|- Query a specific data stream, not a broad `logs-*`: on large clusters a broad pattern scans
23|  every data stream and times out. Find candidates with
24|  `GET /_resolve/index/<remote>:logs-*<keyword>*`, then query the one you need.
25|- Add `?format=txt` to `_query` for a compact text table instead of JSON. Build the body with
26|  `jq -n --arg q '<ES|QL>' '{query: $q}' | curl … -d @-` so the query needs no JSON escaping,
27|  and put regexes (`GROK`, `RLIKE`) in triple-quoted `"""…"""` strings so backslashes stay
28|  literal.
29|- Bound every telemetry query with a `@timestamp` range and every curl with `--max-time 120`.
30|  If a query times out, filter on a structured field (`data_stream.dataset`, `host.name`) before
31|  any text match, or split the window into hours or days.
32|- Never hide a failure: no `2>/dev/null`, `|| true`, or piping a response straight into `jq`.
33|  A failed request then looks like no data. Check for `.error` first.
34|- The sandbox has `jq` and `python3`; there is no `python`.
35|- Common ES|QL mistakes: `LIKE` wildcards are `*`, not `%`; string comparisons are
36|  case-sensitive; use `MATCH_PHRASE(message, "…")` for text; count conditionally with
37|  `COUNT(*) WHERE …`; `first` and `last` are reserved; convert fields with conflicting types with
38|  `TO_STRING`; `KEEP` only the columns you need when fetching rows.
39|- More ES|QL traps: numeric-looking fields such as `http.response.status_code` may be `keyword`
40|  (compare with `TO_INTEGER(…)`); integer division truncates, so write `100.0 * a / b`; `==` and
41|  `!=` never match null, so count nulls with `IS NULL`; quote field names containing `/` or `-`
42|  in backticks; without `LIMIT`, results stop at 1000 rows.
43|- Before querying a field, check which streams map it with
44|  `_field_caps?fields=<field>&include_unmapped=true`: the response then lists the indices for
45|  each type, including `unmapped`. `Unknown column [x]` means no index in the `FROM` pattern
46|  maps `x`: pick another stream instead of retrying. Prefer `_count` or ES|QL `STATS` for
47|  totals and a small `LIMIT` for raw documents.
48|
49|```bash
50|# connector_id must be set on every one of these commands
51|curl --fail-with-body -sS --max-time 120 -H "Authorization: $CONNECTOR_HEADER_AUTHORIZATION" \
52|  "$CONNECTOR_CONFIG_URL/_remote/info"
53|
54|curl --fail-with-body -sS --max-time 120 -H "Authorization: $CONNECTOR_HEADER_AUTHORIZATION" \
55|  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
56|  "$CONNECTOR_CONFIG_URL/_query?format=txt" \
57|  -d '{"query":"FROM logs-* | WHERE @timestamp >= \"2026-01-01T00:00:00Z\" AND @timestamp < \"2026-01-01T01:00:00Z\" | STATS count = COUNT(*) BY service.name | SORT count DESC | LIMIT 20"}'
58|
59|# Find the data streams that match a keyword on one remote
60|curl --fail-with-body -sS --max-time 120 -H "Authorization: $CONNECTOR_HEADER_AUTHORIZATION" \
61|  "$CONNECTOR_CONFIG_URL/_resolve/index/<remote>:logs-*nginx*"
62|
63|# Count one data stream on every remote whose name starts with logging-, 8 at a time, each line
64|# prefixed with its remote; failed requests print their error
65|q() {
66|  curl --fail-with-body -sS --max-time 30 -H "Authorization: $CONNECTOR_HEADER_AUTHORIZATION" \
67|    -H "Content-Type: application/json" "$CONNECTOR_CONFIG_URL/_query?format=txt" \
68|    -d "{\"query\":\"FROM $1:logs-nginx.error-* | WHERE @timestamp >= \\\"2026-01-01T00:00:00Z\\\" AND @timestamp < \\\"2026-01-01T06:00:00Z\\\" | STATS count = COUNT(*)\"}" \
69|    2>&1 | sed "s/^/$1\t/"
70|}
71|export -f q
72|curl --fail-with-body -sS --max-time 120 -H "Authorization: $CONNECTOR_HEADER_AUTHORIZATION" \
73|  "$CONNECTOR_CONFIG_URL/_remote/info" | jq -r 'keys[] | select(startswith("logging-"))' \
74|  | xargs -P 8 -n 1 bash -c 'q "$0"'
75|```

response.message:
**Root cause confirmed:** The `paymentUnreachable` feature flag in flagd was switched to `on` from 21:20 to 22:50 UTC on 2026-04-22, which injected a DNS resolution failure (`lookup badAddress on 127.0.0.11:53: server misbehaving`) into the checkout service's call to the payment service. Every `PlaceOrder` attempt during that window failed instantly (17-68ms) at the payment-charge step, before any charge, order write, or cart mutation occurred — matching exactly the symptoms reported (immediate error, user kept on cart page, no payment/order/cart changes, ~50ms resolution).

The evidence is tight: 124 flag resolutions of `paymentUnreachable=on` line up exactly with 124 `PlaceOrder` failures carrying the DNS error, and the flag's on/off transitions align to the minute with the start and end of the 100% failure window. The payment service's own CPU/memory metrics stayed flat throughout, ruling out an internal payment-service fault — it was a downstream victim of the injected network issue, not the root cause. A separate, pre-existing low-rate "Invalid token" loyalty-card defect in payment was dismissed as unrelated (continuous before/during/after, doesn't explain the spike).

I've recorded a proposal to confirm whether this flag toggle was intentional (e.g., chaos testing) or accidental, revert it if unintentional, and add alerting on this flag staying "on" in production.

input.message: Why did the error come back so fast, in about 50 ms?

response.message:
The fast ~50ms failure is explained directly by where in the call chain the fault was injected, and I can show you the concrete numbers from the trace data.

**What happened mechanically:**

The DNS lookup for `badAddress` fails essentially instantly — it's not a network timeout where a client waits for a connection attempt to a real host to time out (which would typically take seconds). Instead, `127.0.0.11:53` (the local DNS resolver, in this case the Docker/container embedded resolver) immediately returns a `server misbehaving` error for a hostname it can't resolve. gRPC/Go's resolver treats that as an immediate, terminal failure rather than something to retry-with-backoff, so the `oteldemo.PaymentService/Charge` call never even gets to opening a TCP connection — it fails at the name-resolution step before any network round-trip to a real payment pod happens.

**What the telemetry shows:**

The 124 failed `PlaceOrder` spans carrying this DNS error had durations ranging from **17ms to 68ms**, averaging **~33ms** — consistent with "resolver immediately says no" rather than any kind of connection or request timeout. For comparison, a normal successful `PlaceOrder` (which does a real charge, writes the order, empties the cart, and publishes to Kafka) takes meaningfully longer because it does real work across multiple downstream calls.

So the speed itself is a fingerprint of the failure mode: a DNS resolution error is a cheap, local, synchronous failure returned by the resolver stub, not a round-trip failure against a live but slow/unreachable service. That's also why no payment was attempted and no order or cart mutation occurred — the call aborted before checkout's code got a response (or lack of one) from an actual payment process it could act on.

response.message:
No. Every single `oteldemo.PaymentService/Charge` call made by checkout during the 21:20–22:50 UTC window (127 calls across the window, all 10-minute buckets) came back as an error — 100%, zero successes. I confirmed this three independent ways in the telemetry:

- **Trace spans**: every `PaymentService/Charge` span in the window has `status.code == Error`, none succeeded.
- **Payment service logs**: zero `"Transaction complete."` log lines from the payment service during the window (that's the line it logs only after it actually processes a charge).
- **Checkout logs/attributes**: zero `"payment went through"` log lines and zero spans with `app.payment.charged = true` on the checkout side.

This lines up with the mechanism already established: the DNS failure happened at name resolution, before the gRPC call ever reached the payment service's process. So the payment service never even received these charge requests — it has no record of them at all, successful or failed. No money moved, no cards were charged, for any of the ~124 failed checkout attempts in this window.
